title: Capacity failsafe and spline reservoir design notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an experimental design for a capacity "spline reservoir" and an accompanying failsafe/soft-recall control plane for Dedicated pools. Goal: give tenants predictable latency floors while enabling opportunistic burst and graceful degradation with minimal manual operational intervention.

High-level idea (one-liner):
Model available headroom as a time-varying smooth reservoir (spline-based curve) that can be fractionally allocated, hedged, and recalled in stages to balance latency budgets, cost, and tenant isolation.

Motivation / pain we're solving:
- Hard to balance deterministic reserved capacity with ephemeral burst demand without blowing cost or causing noisy-neighbor incidents.
- Current binary reserve (reserved vs on-demand) leads to big step-changes when demand spikes — poor tail latency.
- Ops manually tune warm pools and prewarming rules; want automated, observable, and reversible policies.

Core concepts (vocabulary; please adopt for discussions):
- Spline reservoir: a smoothed curve that represents available headroom over time (minutes->hours). Constructed from historical demand + forecast + explicit commitments.
- Hedged commitments: portions of reservations that are convertible to burst credits under controlled conditions (partial liquidity).
- Soft-recall: staged reclaiming of hedged credits using graceful fidelity reductions, not hard evictions.
- Latency-budgeted allocation: each tenant exposes a latency percentile (p95/p99) budget; allocation tries to satisfy budgets first then distributes remnant headroom.
- Fidelity lanes: ordered degradation paths (full fidelity -> compressed quantization model -> lightweight model -> queue) for controlled quality loss during recall.

Design sketch:
1) Signals we ingest
   - Per-tenant QPS, token/s, recent tail latencies (p50,p95,p99), model type, concurrency patterns
   - Infra signals: GPU utilization, thermal headroom, node churn, warm-pool counts
   - Business signals: committed reserved units, contract hedges, SLA tiers

2) Spline reservoir construction
   - Build a short-term forecast (5m, 1h, 6h) using ETS + simple LSTM ensemble for burstiness features
   - Fit a constrained cubic spline over forecast + committed minimums to create a smooth headroom curve
   - Spline properties: monotonic where appropriate, enforce non-negative, allow configurable smoothness parameter per-region

3) Allocation / hedging policy
   - Base allocation: satisfy guaranteed reservations (hard floor).
   - Hedged band: a middle band of capacity that can be offered as burst credits with probability-weighted recall cost charged back to customer if recalled frequently.
   - Opportunistic layer: slack that can be used by best-effort tenants; throttled first on recall.
   - Assignment rules use latency budgets prioritized by SLA tier and weighted by recent regression signals.

4) Soft-recall flow (operator & system flow)
   - Triggering events: node pressure above threshold, predicted shortfall from spline forecast, or operator-initiated emergency.
   - Stage 0 (gentle): increase batching, apply KV prefix caching aggressively, request app-level rate smoothing (if tenant supports client-side backoff/hedge).
   - Stage 1 (fidelity lane): move some model invocations to lower-fidelity variant (quantized / smaller model).
   - Stage 2 (deferred work): delay non-interactive requests and push to queue with estimated retry window.
   - Stage 3 (soft-recall): reclaim hedged credits in time-sliced windows; apply reduced throughput allowances rather than immediate eviction.
   - Stage 4 (hard): last resort preemption with service-level credits and notifications.

5) Isolation controls and fairness
   - Per-tenant fast-path tokens: ephemeral token that indicates entitlement to low-latency lane. Revoke to throttle specific tenants without pool-wide impact.
   - Isolation score: computed per-tenant from recent noisy-neighbor signals; score used to decay hedged credit eligibility.
   - Fair smoothing: exponential decay of reclaimed capacity so tenants experience a gradual ramp-down rather than oscillations.

6) Autoscaler integration (how this plugs into autoscaling):
   - Autoscaler gets input from spline reservoir (effective slack) instead of raw util numbers when deciding prewarm actions.
   - Predictive warm-pool spawns are gated by hedged credit burn rate and thermal constraints.
   - Autoscale cooldowns adjusted dynamically by current soft-recall stage to avoid flip-flopping.

Operational runbook (draft):
- Normal: monitor reservoir smoothness and hedged burn rate; alert if burn rate > 0.75 for 10m
- Shortfall predicted: autoscaler prewarm triggered with conservative headroom; send preliminary tenant emails for hedged recall window > 30m
- In-flight soft-recall: ops page with per-tenant degradation map, ability to pause recall for a tenant for 10m (safety), manual escalate to Stage 4
- Post-incident: run regression on p99 latency and hedged recall frequency; adjust hedged pricing and allocation smoothing.

Metrics and SLOs to track (proposed):
- p50/p95/p99 per-tenant during normal vs recall windows (strings: p95_recall_delta)
- Hedged credit burn rate (fraction of hedged pool consumed per hour)
- Recall frequency per tenant (target < 1 per week for premium tenants)
- Smoothness metric: L2 norm between raw forecast and spline (lower is smoother)
- Warm-pool efficiency: prewarm success rate vs cost
- User-visible degradation incidents (count, duration)

Experiment plan (MVP -> alpha -> beta):
- MVP (4 weeks): offline prototype of spline construction & allocation simulator. Run replay on 6 weeks of traffic to validate recall decisions.
- Alpha (8 weeks): deploy read-only to production to compute recommendations; surface dashboard with simulated recall impacts. Collect ops feedback.
- Beta (12 weeks): enable soft-recall for non-critical tenants in one region; metrics + rollback hooks; collect customer impact and pick pricing adjustments.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Billing: how to charge for hedged credits that are recalled often? immediate refund vs credit ledger? (ops + finance input needed)
- Model fidelity transitions: do we require model authors to provide fidelity variants or do we run quantized on-the-fly? (research + infra feasibility)
- Fairness constraints: how to prevent rich tenants gaming hedged credits? economic penalties vs hard limits?
- Complexity vs transparency: will customers accept probabilistic capacity descriptions (spline) vs fixed numbers? need comms plan.

Next steps / owner action items:
- (Sofia) spin up replay harness for last 8 weeks of production traffic, target dataset sanitization by 2025-02-17
- (Miguel) prototype spline fitter and open-source small library for constrained cubic splines by 2025-02-24
- (Priya) draft billing experiment proposal for hedged credits with Finance by 2025-02-26
- (Jordan) draft a minimal control-plane API for hedged credit lifecycle (allocate/commit/recall/appeal) by 2025-03-03

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Think about a visualization: "reservoir band" stacked chart with committed floor, hedged band, opportunistic band + predicted shortfall overlay. Very helpful for sales and SRE runbooks.
- Consider a short-term leasing market for hedged capacity where customers bid for more reliability within a time window. Probably for later.

References / links:
- See linked artifacts above for Confluence primer and ENG-3482 for initial autoscaler interface.
- Related reading: "fractional reserve systems" internal notes (search drive: fractional-reserve*), prior thermal autoscaler notes in this folder.

This is intentionally fuzzy — the aim is to surface new language and an experimentation runway that avoids yet another incremental autoscaler tweak. Feedback welcome.
